unit.title: Real-data challenges
unit.description: Predict, mark levels and trade on real charts to see what actually happened

texts: Up or down?
30 real daily candles from a stock. Decide whether, **10 sessions later**, the price was higher or lower, and see what happened.
If you flipped a coin instead of looking at the chart, how many out of 10 would you get right, on average?
None
About 5
All 10
Guessing at random gets **half** right, on average. To know whether you're doing better than a coin, you need lots of attempts.
Play all five rounds.
In the short term, price has a lot of **noise**: in two weeks, one piece of news can change everything. **What you do control is how much you risk.**
Well done! Skill or luck? With five attempts, there's no way to tell.
Done. Was it easier or harder than you expected?
Look at the trend, where the price is and the size of the candles
Seven out of ten
Leo
I got 7 out of 10 right on «up or down?»!
I've found my method. Tomorrow I'm putting my savings in.
What do you tell him?
Go for it! 7 out of 10 is a foolproof method
Flipping a coin, you get 7 out of 10 or more 17 % of the time.
With 10 attempts, luck rules: you need many more
That's it. You need dozens or hundreds of attempts to tell skill from luck.
Try it with half your savings first
Less risk, but the same 10-attempt test: it still tells you nothing.
And beware the gambler's fallacy: no session is ever «due».

steps.title: What to look at before deciding
steps.body:
• **Prior trend:** higher highs and higher lows, or lower ones?
• **Where the price is:** near the highs, near the lows or in the middle?
• **Candle size:** big candles = more volatility = more uncertainty.

None of this guarantees the outcome: in two weeks, a single piece of news can change everything. Note down whether you get each chart right. With only a few attempts, luck rules.
steps.key: In the short term, price is mostly noise: what you do control is how much you risk.
steps.tip: Try it: add a stock to Favourites, predict whether it rises and check in two weeks.

texts: Up or down? Crypto
Real daily candles from bitcoin and ethereum: **10 days later**, higher or lower? Crypto never closes: it trades **24 hours a day, 7 days a week**.
Play all four rounds.

Bitcoin has an annual volatility of **50–80 %**, compared with ~15 % for a global stock index, and it has fallen more than 70 % from its highs several times. It isn't regulated like a deposit: **you can lose everything you've invested**.
All four moved more than 8 % in just 10 days.
Look at the size of the candles before deciding
More volatile, smaller size
You have **€10,000** and risk **1 %** per trade at most: €100. On a calm stock the stop can go at 3 %, but in crypto the noise forces you to move it further away.
If you move the stop from 3 % to 10 % while risking the same, how much can you buy?
More
The same
Quite a bit less
The same €100 of risk: with the stop at 3 %, about €3,333; at 10 %, only **€1,000**.
Set the stop at 10 %, typical for a crypto, with 1 % risk.
**The more volatile the asset, the further away the stop and the smaller the position.** That way, even if it's hit, you lose the same.
With that much risk, ten losses in a row leave your account badly dented.
Stop far away, small position. That way one bad day won't sink you.
Move the stop distance

steps.title: What it takes to recover
steps.body:
• If it falls **50 %**, it has to rise **+100 %** to get back to where it started.
• If it falls **80 %**, **+400 %**: multiply by 5.

Bitcoin has fallen more than 70 % from its highs several times.
steps.key: Big falls are very hard to recover from: in crypto, only use money you could afford to lose entirely.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open bitcoin and see how much it moved in the last week.

u35l3.title: Up or down? Currencies and gold

texts: Gold in dollars, gains in euros
You buy **€1,000** of gold from Spain and gold rises 10 %. Have you made 10 %? Gold **is priced in dollars**: what the dollar does against the euro also counts.
dollar
Gold rises 10 % in dollars, but the dollar falls 10 % against the euro. What do you make in euros?
More or less nothing
1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99: **−1 %**. What gold gains, the currency eats up.
Find a case where gold rises in dollars and you lose in euros.
In euros, both the asset **and the currency** count. And what moves currencies most is **interest rates** and each country's economic surprises.
In euros, you lose. Look at what the dollar did.
Move gold and the dollar
Up or down? Currencies and metals
Real daily candles from currencies, gold and silver: **10 sessions later**, higher or lower? Check the scale carefully.
Play all five rounds.
Major currencies don't move much: **2 % in two weeks is already a lot**. Metals move quite a bit more: gold is driven by interest rates, the dollar and fear, and none of that shows up in 30 candles.
Currencies: less than 2 %. Gold and silver: more than 9 %.
Check the axis scale before deciding

steps.title: Gold, a safe haven with caveats
steps.body:
A pair like **EUR/USD** tells you how many dollars one euro is worth: if it goes from 1.10 to 1.12, the euro has appreciated against the dollar.

Gold pays no interest or dividends. People tend to turn to it in crises and against inflation, but it can go years without rising: from 1980 to 2000 it lost a lot of value in real terms.

With currencies, check the axis scale carefully: 1 % is already a lot.
steps.key: Safe haven doesn't mean it always goes up: it means lots of people buy it when they're scared.
steps.tip: Try it: in Market, open EUR/USD and see how much it has moved in a month.

steps.prompt: Warm-up: tap the hammer (small body at the top and a long lower wick, after a fall).
steps.ok: That's it! Sellers pushed the price down and buyers brought it back up.
steps.ko: Look for the candle whose lower wick is much longer than its body.

steps.prompt: Now tap the candle that completes the bearish engulfing: a red body that swallows the previous green one, after a rise.
steps.ok: That's it! Sellers wiped out the whole of the previous day in one go.
steps.ko: Look for a red candle whose body completely covers the green body before it.

texts: What does each candle tell you?
Each pattern suggests something **depending on where it appears**. Does it point to a possible upward reversal, a downward one or indecision?
Possible upward reversal
Possible downward reversal
Indecision
Hammer after a fall
Long lower wick: buyers rejected the low prices.
Shooting star after a rise
Long upper wick: sellers pushed the price back down.
Doji: open almost equal to close
Nobody won the session. Wait for the next candle.
Bullish engulfing after a fall
A green body swallows the previous red one.
The shape of a hammer, but after a rise
That's the hanging man: same shape, different context.
Morning star: big red, small one, strong green
Three candles that say buyers are taking charge.
Bearish engulfing after a rise
A red body swallows the previous green one.
Sort the seven patterns.
**A pattern is a clue, not an order**: many fail. It's confirmed by the context and the next candle, and always with a stop.
First look at where the price is coming from: was it rising or falling?
Sort each pattern

steps.title: Pattern cheat sheet
steps.body:
• **Hammer:** long lower wick after a fall.
• **Shooting star:** long upper wick after a rise.
• **Doji:** open ≈ close.
• **Engulfing:** one body swallows the previous one, in the opposite direction.
• **Marubozu:** long body with hardly any wicks.
• **Morning star:** a big red, a small one and a strong green.

Before looking for the candle, check where the price is coming from.
steps.key: A pattern is a clue, not an order: confirm it with the context.
steps.tip: Try it: open a stock with daily candles and look for a hammer after a fall.

texts: Trade with the support
Real candles: the price has a **support** 3 % below your entry and a **resistance** 6 % above. Place your stop and your target.
Put the stop below the support and the target near the resistance. Then see what happened.

A **support** is an area where the price has stopped falling several times (buyers step in); a **resistance** is where it has stopped rising. **They give your stop and target a logical place**, though nothing guarantees they'll hold.
Your stop is above the support: noise could trigger it.
Target hit! This time the support held.
Find the floor on the chart and put the stop below it
Support broken?
Nuria
My share has been bouncing off the same floor for months.
Today it closed just a hair below. Support broken! I'm selling everything.
What do you tell her?
Yes, sell before it crashes
Maybe. But many breakouts are false: they cross for a few days and come back.
Wait and see if it closes several sessions below, with volume
Good. That filters out lots of false breakouts.
Buy more: it's cheaper now
If the support really breaks, «cheaper» can get a lot cheaper.
Two days later, the price is back inside the range.
A **false breakout**. That's why supports are **zones**, not lines.
And if they really break, they swap roles: broken resistance becomes support.

steps.title: How to find them
steps.body: Look for the lows and highs that stand out most and check whether the price has come back to them. The more often a level holds, the more people watch it. But many breakouts are **false**: the price crosses for a few days and then comes back inside. Draw wide zones, not thin lines: the market doesn't use a ruler.
steps.key: A support is where buyers showed up before; nothing guarantees they'll come back.
steps.tip: Try it: mark a support on a stock's chart and set an alert there.

texts: Place your stop
Real candles: you've bought at the last price and the last significant low is **1.6 %** below. Where do you put the stop and the target?
Stop below the low, with some margin, and a target at least twice as far. Then see what happened.
The stop goes **where your idea stops making sense**: just below the last significant low, with a margin for noise. The target, near the previous high: many traders won't enter below **2:1**.
The stop was hit. Was it too close to the low?
Target hit! The stop with some margin rode out the noise.
Your target isn't even twice your risk. Is it worth it?
Place the stop and the target
The price is closing in on the stop
Laura
I bought with my stop below the last low. And now the price is falling…
It's about to touch it. Should I lower it a bit to give it some room?
What do you tell her?
Yes, lower it: it's bound to bounce
That's how a small, planned loss turns into a big one. It's the disposition effect.
Leave it: that was the point where your idea stopped working
That's it. If it's hit, you lose what you planned and move on to the next one.
Buy more to lower your average price
You're doubling down on an idea the market is proving wrong.
You decide the stop in cold blood, before entering. Never move it against you.

steps.title: Stop first, then size
steps.body:
Size = (capital × % risk) ÷ (entry − stop).

With €10,000 and 1 % risk, you're risking €100. Entry at €50 and stop at €47: 100 ÷ 3 = **33 shares** (about €1,650).

A stop that's too tight gets hit by normal noise; one that's too far away forces you to buy very little.
steps.key: You don't decide how much to buy: the distance to your stop does.
steps.tip: Try it: on your next purchase in the simulator, place the stop below the last low.

texts: Record profits
Marta
My company has just reported record profits!
And its share price drops 8 %. What kind of joke is this?
What happened?
The market expected even more
That's it. The price already included what was expected, and a record can still disappoint.
Someone made a mistake publishing the price
There's no mistake: the market compares it with what it expected.
Records always make the share price fall
There's no fixed rule: it depends on what the market expected.
By the time you read the headline, thousands of people and algorithms have already reacted.
News or surprise?
Prices move on **surprise**, not on news. Did the market already know this, or does it catch it off guard?
Already priced in
Surprise: it could move the price
Record profits, just what analysts expected
If what was expected happens, it was already in the price.
The central bank raises rates more than expected
The unexpected is what moves the price.
The launch of the new phone, announced weeks ago
Everyone knew about it before you did.
Inflation at 3.4 % when 3 % was expected
A worse-than-expected figure tends to weigh on prices in the short term.
A company joins an index, announced weeks earlier
Forced, pre-announced buying tends to move the price before the day itself.
An accounting fraud comes to light out of the blue
Nobody saw it coming: the price adjusts in one go.
Sort the six headlines.
**On the stock market, good news that was already expected isn't news.** Before reacting, ask yourself what the market expected.
Ask yourself: did everyone already know this?
Sort each headline

steps.title: What to do when a headline hits
steps.body:
• Ask yourself what the market **expected**, not whether the news is good or bad.
• Don't trade in the first few minutes: the price jumps and the *spread* widens.
• If you already have a position, let your stop decide, not panic.
steps.key: On the stock market, good news that was already expected isn't news.
steps.tip: Try it: when you see a headline, open the asset in Market and check whether it has already moved.

texts: Stop and target
Real candles: your thesis is that the price bounces off its support, **7.5 %** below your entry. Place the **stop** and the **target**, and see what happened.
Put the stop below the support and see what happened.
This time the stop was hit, but without it, 15 sessions later, you'd have been down 21.8 %. **A good plan doesn't guarantee a win: it guarantees that, if you lose, you lose what you planned.**
The stop was hit. It hurts, but it's exactly what you'd decided to risk.
Your stop is above the support.
Find the support and put the stop below it
The size
A **€10,000** account and **1 %** risk (€100), with the stop **8 %** below your entry. How much do you buy?
With the stop at 8 % and 1 % risk, if the stop is hit, how much do you lose?
Everything you invested
You only buy **€1,250** (100 ÷ 8 %). If it's hit, you lose 8 % of that: **€100, or 1R**.
Set the stop at 8 % with 1 % risk.
**You don't decide how much to buy: the distance to your stop does.** What you risk when you enter is **1R**: if you risk €100 and make €250, you've made 2.5R.
€1,250: if the stop is hit, you lose exactly €100.
With more than 2 % per trade, a losing streak really hurts.
Move the stop distance

steps.title: Five decisions before you enter
steps.body:
1. **Thesis:** why you think it could rise.
2. **Stop:** where you're wrong.
3. **Target:** where you take profits.
4. **Size:** how much you buy so you only risk 1 %.
5. **Record:** you log it in your journal.

Measuring in **R** lets you compare trades of different sizes and know whether your system wins in the long run. Review your journal every 20 trades: it shows you what your memory would rather forget.
steps.key: A good trade is one that follows the plan, even if it loses.
steps.tip: Try it: make a purchase in the simulator with a stop, a target and 1 % risk.

texts: Does it follow the rules?
Challenge rules, with €10,000 in virtual money: no asset above **40 %**, at least **4 assets**, crypto **10 %** at most and each trade risks **1 %** at most. Does it follow the rules or break one?
Follows the rules
Breaks a rule
MSCI World 40 %, bonds 30 %, gold 20 %, bitcoin 10 %
Four assets, none above 40 % and crypto stays at 10 %.
Bitcoin at 15 % of the portfolio
You could lose all of your crypto: 10 % at most.
Only three assets, in equal parts
You need at least 4.
A trade that risks €80
1 % of €10,000 is €100: €80 is within the limit.
The IBEX 35 ETF at 45 %
No asset can go above 40 %.
A trade that risks €300
That's 3 % of the portfolio: three times the limit.
Check the six cases.
With a maximum of 40 % per asset and at least 4 assets, **no surprise can sink your week**. And keep crypto small: you could lose all of it.
Go over the four rules: weight, number of assets, crypto and risk.
Follows the rules or breaks one?
Tuesday: the market falls
Álex
Tuesday. A worse-than-expected inflation figure comes out and the market falls 3 %.
Your portfolio loses €180: −1.8 %.
Did you see? I'm selling everything before it drops further.
What about you?
I sell all my shares so they don't fall any further
You turn a normal fall into a loss, and then you'll have to guess when to get back in.
I don't touch anything: the portfolio is spread out and the fall is normal
That's it. −1.8 % on a bad day is exactly what it's built for.
I move everything into bitcoin to win it back fast
You break the 10 % rule and you're revenge trading.
The market fell 3 %; your portfolio, only 1.8 %. That's diversification.

steps.title: Your week
steps.body:
The winner isn't whoever gains the most, but whoever **sticks to the rules** and makes decisions they could explain. On Monday you allocate, during the week news and opportunities come up, and on Friday you review.

It's an educational simulation with **€10,000 in virtual money**, not a recommendation.

If you couldn't explain a decision out loud, don't make it.
steps.key: The rules are written on Monday with a cool head; for the rest of the week, you just follow them.
steps.tip: Try it: split your virtual Portfolio using the challenge rules and review it on Friday.

u35l1-1.prompt: Look at the 30 candles. Did the price end up higher or lower 10 sessions later?
u35l1-1.explanation: Over two weeks, the outcome depends heavily on news nobody sees coming. That's why no serious trader trades without a stop: not because they expect to be wrong, but because they know they could be.

u35l1-2.prompt: Another stock, another moment. Higher or lower in 10 sessions' time?
u35l1-2.explanation: Look at the size of the candles: the bigger they are, the more uncertain the next move, in either direction. Volatility tells you how much something moves, not which way.

u35l1-3.prompt: No predicting the future: what trend did this price have? (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · March–May 2026)
u35l1-3.explanation: Ever higher highs and lows: from about $249 to about $309. Reading the past trend is easy; knowing how long it will last isn't.

u35l1-4.prompt: The last few candles have been intense. Higher or lower 10 sessions later?
u35l1-4.explanation: After a strong move, your brain is tempted by two opposite ideas: «it'll keep going» (recency bias) or «it's due to turn» (gambler's fallacy). Neither is reliable on its own.

u35l1-6.prompt: European stock, daily candles. Did it go up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u35l1-6.explanation: When the price is in the middle of its recent range, there isn't even a clear level to watch or a logical place for a stop. In those cases, not trading is also a decision.

u35l1-8.prompt: What trend do you see in this stretch? (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · December 2025 – February 2026)
u35l1-8.explanation: Ever lower highs and lows: from about $488 to about $384. In a downtrend, «it's already cheap» isn't an argument: it can get cheaper.

u35l1-9.prompt: If a stock has risen 5 days in a row, it's more likely to fall on the sixth.
u35l1-9.explanation: That's the gambler's fallacy: sessions don't «owe» each other anything. A streak doesn't make a change of direction more likely.

u35l2-3.prompt: Another cryptocurrency. Higher or lower 10 days later?
u35l2-3.explanation: The big cryptos tend to move in the same direction as bitcoin, often more sharply. Holding several barely reduces your risk: when one falls, they usually fall together.

u35l2-4.prompt: Bruno sees that a crypto has gone up 40 % in a week and social media is talking about nothing else. He has €1,000 set aside for next month's rent. What does he do?
options: Takes out a loan to put in even more
Leaves the rent money alone; if he wants to try, he only uses money he could lose entirely
Puts in the €1,000 before it goes up even more
u35l2-4.explanation: FOMO pushes you to buy after a big rise and with money you shouldn't touch. In crypto, only use money you could afford to lose completely.
feedback: Debt to buy the most volatile asset on the market: if it falls, he still owes the money and no longer has the crypto.
Good: only money whose total loss wouldn't change your life goes into crypto.
It's his rent money. If it drops 30 % in a few days, as it has many times, he can't pay. Textbook FOMO.

u35l2-6.prompt: November 2021: bitcoin hits all-time highs above $65,000, and a few weeks earlier the first bitcoin futures ETF launched in the US. What did the price do over the following year?
u35l2-6.explanation: When an asset is at its highs and on every front page, the feeling of safety is at its peak, but that optimism is already in the price. Always ask yourself how much you'd lose if you're wrong, not just how much you could make.

u35l2-9.prompt: If your portfolio holds two different cryptocurrencies, it's already well diversified.
u35l2-9.explanation: The big cryptos tend to move together. Diversifying means combining different assets (shares, bonds, cash…), not two pieces from the same game.

u35l2-10.prompt: The first crypto is back, at a different time. Higher or lower 10 days later?
u35l2-10.explanation: In crypto, the price can crash or soar on a Saturday night too. That's why many people leave stop orders in place instead of watching the screen around the clock.

u35l3-1.prompt: EUR/USD goes from 1.08 to 1.12. What has happened?
options: The dollar has appreciated against the euro
The euro has appreciated against the dollar
Both have lost the same amount of value
u35l3-1.explanation: EUR/USD = how many dollars one euro costs. If it takes more dollars to buy one euro, the euro is worth more.

u35l3-2.prompt: Currency pair, daily candles. Higher or lower 10 sessions later?
u35l3-2.explanation: Look at the scale: in currencies, what looks like a crash may be 1 %. That's why forex brokers offer so much leverage… and why so many people lose money with it.

u35l3-4.prompt: Precious metal, daily candles. Did it go up or down over the next 10 sessions?
u35l3-4.explanation: Gold has no earnings to value: it's moved by interest rates, the dollar and fear. None of the three shows up on a 30-candle chart.

u35l3-5.prompt: Look at the visible stretch of gold up to August 2020. What trend did it have? (Gold · weekly closes · up to the week of 03/08/2020)
u35l3-5.explanation: From about $1,200 to over $2,000 an ounce in two years, with higher highs and higher lows: a textbook uptrend.

u35l3-6.prompt: Another currency pair. Higher or lower 10 sessions later?
u35l3-6.explanation: The yen has been used as a safe haven in times of fear, and Japanese interest rates were well below US rates for years. That interest-rate gap moves the pair more than any candle.

u35l3-7.prompt: Over the medium term, what usually moves a major currency the most?
options: Interest rates and economic surprises in its country
u35l3-7.explanation: If a central bank raises rates more than expected, its currency tends to attract money. Candles reflect those changes; they don't cause them.

u35l4-1.explanation: A small body at the top and a lower wick at least twice the size of the body, after several down candles. (NVIDIA · daily candles · June 2026)

u35l4-2.explanation: A long upper wick and a small body at the bottom, after a rise: buyers tried, and sellers pushed the price back down. (Microsoft · daily candles · April 2026)

u35l4-3.prompt: Match each candle with what it tells you.
u35l4-3.explanation: Each candle sums up a battle between buyers and sellers: the body tells you who won, and the wicks how far the other side got.
right: One side dominated the whole session

u35l4-4.explanation: Open and close almost equal, with wicks on both sides: indecision. Wait for the next candle before drawing conclusions. (Apple · daily candles · September 2026)

u35l4-5.prompt: Tap the candle that completes the bullish engulfing.
u35l4-5.explanation: A green candle whose body completely engulfs the previous red body, after a fall. (Apple · daily candles · April 2025)

u35l4-8.prompt: A hammer guarantees that the price is going to rise.
u35l4-8.explanation: It's a clue to a possible reversal, not a guarantee: many patterns fail. That's why you wait for the next candle and place a stop below the wick.

u35l4-9.explanation: A long green body with almost no wicks: buyers were in charge from the start of the session to the end. (Apple · daily candles · June–July 2026)

u35l4-10.prompt: Tap the third candle of the morning star.
u35l4-10.explanation: First a big red one, then a small one showing doubt, and finally a strong green one that closes above the midpoint of the first. (Microsoft · daily candles · January–February 2026)

u35l5-1.prompt: Sideways range. Tap the lowest point: the floor buyers are watching. (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · September–November 2024)
u35l5-1.explanation: About $222: the bottom of the range marks the support. If the price comes back there, lots of people will watch whether it holds.

u35l5-2.prompt: Now the ceiling: tap the highest point of this range. (Microsoft · closes every 3 sessions · August–October 2024)
u35l5-2.explanation: About $433: that's where the rises stalled. It's the resistance of the range.

u35l5-3.prompt: An area where the price has stopped falling several times is called ____.
u35l5-3.explanation: Buyers show up at support; sellers, at resistance.

u35l5-4.prompt: Stock index, daily candles. Look at where the price is relative to its recent lows. Higher or lower 10 sessions later?
u35l5-4.explanation: Being close to support doesn't guarantee a bounce: it may hold or it may break. What it does give you is a logical place for your stop if you're wrong.

u35l5-5.prompt: Downtrend. Tap the low: the level buyers will have to defend. (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · February–April 2025)
u35l5-5.explanation: About $172: after that low there was a bounce. A low like that becomes a reference point for the future.

u35l5-8.prompt: Another index. Can you see a clear floor near the current price? Decide: higher or lower 10 sessions later?
u35l5-8.explanation: If there's no clear support nearby, the stop would have to go far away and the trade would have a worse reward-to-risk ratio. Sometimes the best move is not to trade.

u35l5-9.prompt: Sideways range with one rebel candle. Tap the low. (NVIDIA · closes every 3 sessions · December 2025 – February 2026)
u35l5-9.explanation: About $174: the price broke below the range for a moment and quickly came back inside. That's a false breakout, and it's why supports are zones, not lines.

u35l6-1.prompt: Before buying, check the trend. What is it? (NVIDIA · closes every 3 sessions · March–May 2026)
u35l6-1.explanation: Higher highs and higher lows: from about $168 to highs of about $236. Buying with the trend and placing the stop below the last low is the classic approach.

u35l6-2.prompt: You've bought at the last price. Place your stop loss where your idea stops being valid.
u35l6-2.explanation: Just below the last significant low (about $408), with a small margin. If the price loses that floor, the trend you were looking for is gone.

u35l6-3.prompt: Now the target: place your take profit.
u35l6-3.explanation: Near the previous high (about $195): that's where sellers showed up last time. Aiming much higher means hoping for something the price hasn't done yet.

u35l6-5.prompt: Place the stop for this purchase.
u35l6-5.explanation: Below the recent low (about €12.90). Not right next to the price, because noise would trigger it, nor so far away that the loss gets out of hand.

u35l6-7.prompt: You have €10,000 and risk at most 1 %. Place the stop and choose the amount.
u35l6-7.explanation: First the stop below the last low; then the amount, so that if it's hit you lose €100 at most. The outcome depends on the market; the risk depends on you.

u35l6-9.prompt: Place the target for this trade.
u35l6-9.explanation: Near the previous high (about $256). If the price breaks through it strongly, you can always raise your stop and let the profit run.

u35l7-2.prompt: March 2020: Covid has put half the world in lockdown and the S&P 500 has fallen more than 30 % in a month. The headlines talk about the worst crisis in decades. What did the index do over the following months?
u35l7-2.explanation: The stock market moves on what it expects from the future, not on today's headlines. When the news is terrible, the key question is whether what's coming will be worse or better than what the price already reflects.

u35l7-3.prompt: Pablo reads on his phone: «The Federal Reserve raises rates more than expected». The index falls 2 % in minutes and Pablo has an open position with his stop in place. What does he do?
options: Lets his plan work: the stop already sets how much he's willing to lose
Buys more because «it's bound to bounce»
Sells everything at market right now, before it falls further
u35l7-3.explanation: In the minutes after a news release, the price moves in jumps and costs go up. Decisions made beforehand, calmly, tend to be better.
